Removing `encoding="utf-8"` from `read_text()` while keeping `errors="ignore"` does not change observable behavior on any platform where Python's default locale encoding is UTF-8 (all modern Linux, macOS, and Windows CI environments). Python 3.15+ even makes UTF-8 mode the universal default. Since `errors="ignore"` is present in both versions, any bytes that would cause a decoding error are silently discarded regardless of which encoding is used. No test running in a standard environment can observe a difference between these two calls.

Path.read_text(encoding="utf-8") and Path.read_text(encoding="UTF-8") produce byte-for-byte identical decoded output for any input file. There is no observable difference in behavior, so no test could ever distinguish the original from the mutant.

Python encoding names are case-insensitive by specification. `"UTF-8"` and `"utf-8"` resolve to the same `codecs.CodecInfo` object, so `file.read_text(encoding="UTF-8", errors="ignore")` is functionally identical to `file.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="ignore")`. The function's return value, exception behaviour, and every downstream observable effect are the same for both spellings. A test that checks the exact string passed to `read_text` would be testing an irrelevant implementation detail (string casing), not real behaviour, and mutmut is not designed to be killed by such mock-based encoding-string checks when the actual codec is identical.

PyYAML 6.x sets `default_flow_style=False` by default in its `Dumper` class (`yaml.Dumper(None).default_flow_style` is `False`). Removing the explicit `default_flow_style=False` from `yaml.dump(...)` therefore changes nothing - the rendered YAML output is byte-for-byte identical for all inputs tested (nested dicts, lists, unicode, long strings, empty dicts, etc.). No test can detect this mutation because there is no observable behavioural difference.

PyYAML's `yaml.dump_all` declares `sort_keys=True` as its default (visible in the function signature `def dump_all(..., sort_keys=True)`). The explicit `sort_keys=True` in the source code is therefore redundant; dropping it leaves the same default in effect. All existing tests (including `test_keys_are_sorted_in_output` and `test_sort_keys_for_determinism`) pass identically against the mutant because the YAML output is byte-for-byte identical.

The `flow` default is unreachable/unobservable. `_PrecommitDumper.increase_indent` overrides `yaml.Dumper.increase_indent`, and it is only ever called by PyYAML's own `Emitter` internals (in `emitter.py`), which always pass `flow` explicitly as a keyword argument at every call site (`self.increase_indent(flow=True)` in expect_flow_sequence/mapping paths, and `self.increase_indent(flow=False, indentless=indentless)` / `self.increase_indent(flow=False)` in block paths). No caller anywhere — in PyYAML or in gpc_init — ever invokes `increase_indent` without specifying `flow`, so the default value is dead code that cannot influence behavior. Additionally, the method body ignores the `indentless` argument entirely (always passes `indentless=False` to `super()`), which is the actual intentional behavior under test, but that logic is untouched by this mutant. Since no test (nor any real call path) can ever hit the default value of `flow`, this mutation is behaviorally equivalent to the original and cannot be killed by any black-box test of the dumper's YAML output.

The `indentless` parameter is never read inside the function body — it is explicitly marked `noqa: ARG002` (unused argument) and the method unconditionally calls `super().increase_indent(flow=flow, indentless=False)`, ignoring whatever value was passed in or defaulted. Additionally, PyYAML always invokes `increase_indent` with explicit keyword arguments internally, never relying on the default. Since the default value can never reach any observable behavior (it's neither used in the body nor triggered by any caller relying on the default), no test can distinguish the mutant from the original code.

PyYAML's base Emitter.increase_indent only branches on the `flow` argument when `self.indent is None`, i.e. exactly once per document, at the very first call made while establishing the root container's indentation; for every subsequent (nested) call `self.indent` is already set, so the code takes the `elif not indentless: self.indent += self.best_indent` path where `flow` plays no role at all, making the mutation unobservable there. `render_yaml` always calls `yaml.dump` on a `dict` with `default_flow_style=False`, so the root container is emitted in block style except in the single special case of an empty top-level dict, which PyYAML always renders as flow style (`{}`). I verified empirically (comparing the original vs. mutated Dumper across `{}`, `{"a": []}`, `{"a": {}}`, `{"a": [], "b": {}}`, `{"repos": []}`, `{"a": [[], {}]}`, `{"a": {"b": {}}}`, and `[]`) that output is byte-for-byte identical in every case: the difference in initial indent value (`best_indent` vs `0`) only matters when there is subsequent content to indent using that value, but an empty flow container `{}`/`[]` has no nested content to display it, and all real (non-empty) containers already pass `flow=False` in both branches since `default_flow_style=False`. Therefore, given how `_PrecommitDumper` is exclusively used inside `render_yaml`, no input produces a detectable difference in output, so the mutant is behaviorally equivalent.

The parent method being called is yaml's Emitter.increase_indent(self, flow=False, indentless=False) — its default value for `indentless` is already False. The original code explicitly passes indentless=False (overriding whatever value the caller/emitter internally intended to pass to this overridden method, which is the whole point of this override — forcing block-style list indentation for pre-commit YAML output). Omitting the keyword and relying on the parent's own default produces the exact same value (False) in every call, since Python fills in the parent's default when the argument is omitted. There is no code path where this default could differ from the explicit value, so the mutation is behaviorally indistinguishable from the original — no test (existing or possible) could observe a difference without relying on implementation internals like inspecting call signatures via mocking, which would be testing implementation detail rather than behavior.

With the project's installed PyYAML version (6.0.3), yaml.Dumper's built-in default for `default_flow_style` is already `False` (PyYAML changed this default from `None` to `False` starting in version 5.1). The `sort_keys` parameter only affects PyYAML's built-in `represent_mapping` sorting logic, which triggers only when the object passed in has a `.items()` method (i.e. is dict-like). `_PrecommitDumper` registers `_semantic_dict_representer` for every `dict` in the tree; that representer always builds an already-ordered plain Python `list` of `(key, value)` tuples (via `_REPO_KEY_ORDER`/`_HOOK_KEY_ORDER` plus alphabetical fallback for the rest) and passes that list to `dumper.represent_mapping`. Since a list has no `.items()` attribute, PyYAML's internal `sort_keys` branch (`if hasattr(mapping, 'items'): ... if self.sort_keys: mapping = sorted(mapping)`) is never reached, so the `sort_keys` flag has no observable effect on output for any dict at any depth. Empirically verified: dumping a dict with unordered keys via `_PrecommitDumper` produces byte-identical YAML with `sort_keys=True` and `sort_keys=False`. No test could observe a difference, so the mutant is equivalent.

render_yaml uses _PrecommitDumper with a custom dict representer (_semantic_dict_representer) registered via add_representer(dict, ...). This representer always builds the node's mapping as a plain Python list of (key, value) tuples ([(k, data[k]) for k in ordered]), not a dict. PyYAML's underlying Representer.represent_mapping only applies dumper.sort_keys when hasattr(mapping, 'items') is True; since a list has no .items(), that sort branch is skipped entirely regardless of the sort_keys flag. Because every dict (top-level and nested) in merged_dict is serialized through this custom representer, the sort_keys parameter passed to yaml.dump has zero effect on output for any input. I verified this empirically: dumping the same test dict with sort_keys=False and sort_keys=True via _PrecommitDumper produced byte-identical YAML output. Therefore no test can ever distinguish this mutant from the original, making it a genuine equivalent mutant.

Python's `importlib.metadata.version()` implements PEP 503 package name normalization: it lowercases the name and collapses `[-_.]` sequences before the filesystem lookup. Therefore `version("PC-INIT")` resolves to exactly the same distribution as `version("pc-init")` and returns the same version string. No test can observe a difference in the output or exit code, making this mutant equivalent. The existing `TestVersion` tests mock `importlib.metadata.version` entirely, so they never exercise the real lookup argument at all.

Path.walk delegates directly to os.walk(root_dir, top_down, on_error, follow_symlinks) with on_error passed through unchanged. Inspecting the CPython os.walk implementation, the error-handling code is exactly: `except OSError as error: if onerror is not None: onerror(error); continue`. Whether on_error is None or a no-op lambda (`lambda _: None`), the observable behavior is identical in every case: on an OSError during scandir, the loop simply continues without recursing into or yielding that directory's contents, and the lambda (when present) does nothing observable anyway (returns None, no side effects). There is no code path where passing None vs. a None-returning lambda produces a different result — both silently ignore scan errors. Hence no test (property-based, unit, or otherwise) could observe a behavioral difference, making this mutant equivalent.

Path.walk's on_error callback (like os.walk's onerror) is invoked purely for its side effect when an OS error occurs while scanning a directory during the walk; its return value is never read, stored, or used to influence control flow by the walk implementation (confirmed via Path.walk docs in the project's Python 3.14 venv). Since the lambda's return value (None vs 0) is discarded either way, there is no way for any test — regardless of whether an error occurs during the walk — to observe a difference between the two mutants. The change is behaviorally unobservable.
